name: Thinset
seoDesc: Thinset: work out total area to be tiled from the length of the area and the width of the area. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and…
summary: Supply the length of the area, the width of the area, the volume needed and the density of thinset and the Thinset calculator solves for total area to be tiled. Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Thinset calculator work?
sections.html:
The Thinset calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total area to be tiled in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the tile size); then you type in the length of the area, the width of the area, the volume needed and the density of thinset.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Thinset calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total area to be tiled=length of the area × width of the area
Total area to be tiled=12 × volume needed ÷ thinset thickness
Weight of thinset needed=(density of thinset × volume needed × (wastage + 1))
Dry material weight=((1 ÷ 100) × dry material percentage × (density of thinset × volume needed × (wastage + 1)))
Bags=rounded up, ((((1 ÷ 100) × dry material percentage × (density of thinset × volume needed × (wastage + 1))) ÷ weight per bag))
Total cost=(cost per bag × rounded up, ((((1 ÷ 100) × dry material percentage × (density of thinset × volume needed × (wastage + 1))) ÷ weight per bag)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • %, opening in percent
  • Mass, opening in kilograms

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Thinset calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length of the area, the width of the area and the volume needed — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Thinset calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total area to be tiled, derived from the length of the area, the width of the area and the volume needed. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Thinset calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length of the area, the width of the area, the volume needed and the density of thinset, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter length of the area in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Length of the area opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Thinset thickness = 0 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Thinset calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
